# Research notes on Proverbs 7

**Scope.** I read Enduring Word (Guzik) in full up to about v. 21, and Precept Austin for vv. 1–3. For the other verses I only had search excerpts from BibleHub and StudyLight, which quote Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Barnes, Poole, Henry, Clarke, Keil & Delitzsch and others. I also found a Bible Odyssey article, one NET Bible note and a bible.org essay. There's very little on vv. 6–7, 11–12, 16–21 and 24–25, so some of those verses only have a note or two. The search tools ran out before I could fill those gaps.

---

## 1. Verse by verse: the traditional reading

**v. 1** — This is the third time in chs. 5–7 that Solomon starts a warning about sexual sin by calling the son to heed God's word. "Treasure" means to hide or store up something you value highly. Precept Austin links it to Ps 119:11. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-7-commentary

**v. 2** — Guzik says Bible reading isn't a magic shield. But someone who really keeps God's commands won't commit this sin, and keeping them starts with knowing them, treasuring them and meditating on them. "Apple of your eye" means the pupil, which the ancients thought was shaped like an apple; we guard God's word the way we guard our eyes (Wiersbe). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/
- Bridges warns that explaining the law away or lowering its demands lets temptation in easily. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-7-commentary

**v. 3** — Precept Austin gives cross-references to Deut 11:18–20, Jer 31:33 and 2 Cor 3:3. Bridges reads it as keeping God's commands close at hand and written on the heart, which God promises to do for his people (Jer 31:33). https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-7-commentary
- JFB: "bind on fingers" pictures inscriptions on rings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-4.htm

**v. 4** — Guzik: the son should have a living relationship with God's word and love it like a sister or close relative. G. Campbell Morgan adds that the love of sisters and pure women friends keeps many men from evil. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/
- Poole: other young men call their mistresses "sisters", so let wisdom be your mistress instead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-4.htm
- Barnes contrasts the adulteress with Wisdom, the true "sister" (same page).
- Cambridge Bible: "kinswoman" literally means "known", i.e. an intimate friend. Elsewhere (Ruth 2:1; 3:2) the word means kinsman (same page).

**v. 5** — The Hebrew word for "strange" has the basic idea of someone you are not related to; in Proverbs the feminine form often means the adulteress. "Smooth words" are tied to her again and again (2:16; 6:24; 7:5). https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-7-commentary
- Matthew Henry: God's word is our defence against her; it shows up sin's tricks and gives answers to its flattery. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_007.cfm

**vv. 6–7** — Solomon tells the story as if watching from his window. "Simple" means inexperienced and gullible, not stupid. Kidner calls the young man featherbrained, exactly the kind who needs borrowed wisdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/
- BibleHub's background note: houses were small and windows faced the street, so watching through a lattice was normal. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/7.htm

**v. 8** — Henry: the youth was idle and wandering about with nothing to do. He links this to Sodom's "abundance of idleness" (Ezek 16:49). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_007.cfm
- Guzik: he leads himself into temptation, step by step. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/

**v. 9** — Trapp, quoted by Guzik: foolish men try to hide from God by hiding God from themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/

**v. 10** — Guzik: she isn't a prostitute, but she dresses like one and has the heart of one. Kidner reads "cunning of heart" (literally "guarded of heart") as meaning she is either hard or secretive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/

**vv. 11–12** — Waltke compares "defiant" to a stubborn cow pulling against restraint (Hos 4:16). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/
- Henry: she hates staying at home and is everywhere except where she should be. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_007.cfm

**v. 13** — "Brazenly" describes contemptuous boldness: a shameless, insolent disregard for God's law, for marriage and for her husband. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-7-commentary
- Guzik: she "caught" him, the language of a trap. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/

**v. 14** — The main reading is religious hypocrisy plus a feast. Gurnall's line is often quoted: she couldn't play the harlot with man until she had played the hypocrite with God. Poole adds that peace-offering meat meant good food was waiting at her house. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/
- Barnes: the offerings had to be eaten the same day, so she invites him to the meal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/7-14.html
- Ellicott: the offerings were split between God, the priests and the offerer, who ate his share as a feast. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/7-14.htm
- Henry: having paid her vows, she thought she had settled her account with God and could start a new tab of sins. Outward religion that doesn't harden people *against* sin hardens them *in* it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_007.cfm

**v. 15** — Wiersbe, quoted by Guzik: she flatters the young man's ego and makes him feel uniquely wanted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/

**vv. 16–17** — Waltke: myrrh, aloes and cinnamon all appear in Song 4:14 as images of sexual love. Trapp: these spices were used on corpses, which should have reminded the youth he was heading to his grave. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/

**v. 18** — Guzik: she misuses the word "love". She offers a kind of love that lasts till morning but ends in misery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/
- Precept Austin: her imagery compares sex to drinking from a fountain, as in Prov 5:18 and Song 4. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-7-commentary

**vv. 19–20** — Guzik: these verses show she is an adulteress, not a harlot. She betrays her husband, her marriage vow and God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/
- Henry: she answers in advance his fear of being caught by the husband. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_007.cfm

**v. 21** — Henry: Wisdom's servants plead with reason and get ignored, while sin wins quickly with lies and flattery. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_007.cfm

**v. 22** — Cambridge: he had been hesitating on the edge and now suddenly jumps. Pulpit: like an ox, he can't see where his action leads. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-22.htm
- Henry: the ox thinks it's being led to pasture. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/7-22.html
- **Text problem.** The KJV's "as a fool to the stocks" only works if two Hebrew words are swapped. Barnes says no attempt to make sense of the present Hebrew is satisfactory. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "as a dog to chains". Pulpit thinks the text is corrupt but falls back on the KJV. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-22.htm
- Precept Austin: on the KJV reading, the stocks stand for public shame. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-7-commentary

**v. 23** — The liver was thought to be where passion sat. Like a bird rushing into a net, he doesn't know his life is at stake. https://biblehub.com/sermons/proverbs/7-22.htm
- Henry: the bird sees only the bait. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/7-22.html

**vv. 24–25** — Henry: never leave the narrow path of virtue for her broad, crowded way. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_007.cfm
- Tyndale commentary, cited by Coffman, gives three defences: guard your mind, keep away, and look past her to the dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/7-27.html

**v. 26** — Henry thinks of Samson and David, strong and wise men brought down by this sin. Barnes pictures a battlefield covered with her dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/7-27.html

**v. 27** — Poole: "Sheol" can mean hell or the grave; he prefers the grave here, though hell follows without repentance. Pulpit: "road" is plural in Hebrew, so there are many ways down but only one end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-27.htm
- Gill: the chambers of death are the deepest parts of hell, the lot of the unrepentant (same page).

---

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

None of the pages I read mark a split between traditions. What I found are differences between individual commentators:

- **v. 14, what her "vows" were.** StudyLight labels Adam Clarke as Wesleyan/Methodist. Clarke thinks she hints that she made a vow for the young man's safety. Gill disagrees: the vows were her own thank-offerings, already made and paid, and had nothing to do with him. Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) gives a reading I didn't see anywhere else: the offering showed she was ritually clean again after her period. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/7-14.html
- **v. 14, use against Rome.** Gill applies the "religious harlot" to the church of Rome, including vows of celibacy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-14.htm
- **v. 4, is Wisdom Christ?** Gill reads "sister/kinsman" as the Gospel and as Christ, our near kinsman-redeemer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-4.htm
  - The bible.org essay is more careful. It says it may go too far to say dogmatically that Wisdom is Christ, but the description leaves room for it. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-two-women-madam-folly-and-dame-wisdom-proverbs-7-9
- **Literal or symbolic woman.** Guzik reads her mainly as a real woman. Bible.org says she is "Madam Folly", a literary device teaching on both a literal and a symbolic level, and that she is shown as the aggressor because she personifies the evil way. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-two-women-madam-folly-and-dame-wisdom-proverbs-7-9

## 3. Other views

- **Modern scholarship (vv. 5, 10–21).** The Hebrew *zarah* can mean strange, loose, alien or foreign. Bible Odyssey sets Proverbs after the return from Babylonian exile. It suggests that, besides being an adulterous wife, she may stand for foreign women, Jewish women who had not been in exile, or worshippers of other gods. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/strange-woman-of-proverbs/
- **v. 4, NET Bible note.** Calling wisdom "sister" prepares for Wisdom being personified in the next two chapters. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=pro&chapter=7&verse=4
- **v. 14, pagan cult.** Coffman cites the Anchor Bible's suggestion that the vows may be linked to sacred prostitution for a fertility goddess. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/7-14.html Clarke points to Eastern gods worshipped in brothels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-7/
- **Catholic and Orthodox.** I didn't reach newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The only related points are secondhand:
  - Pulpit notes that the Book of Wisdom (ch. 8) pictures Wisdom as a wife, and quotes the Vulgate's different wording of v. 22. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-4.htm, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/7-22.htm
  - Pulpit also says "spiritual writers" see the seductions of false doctrine in v. 27. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/7-27.htm
- **Prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace.** I found nothing on these sites that connects them to this chapter.
